'''Ceva''', the ancient '''Ceba''', is a small [[Italy|Italian]] town in the [[province of Cuneo]], region of [[Piedmont]], {{convert|49|km|mi}} east of [[Cuneo]]. It lies on the right bank of the [[Tanaro River|Tanaro]] on a wedge of land between that river and the Cevetta stream.

==History==
In the pre-Roman period the territory around Ceva was inhabited by the branch of the mountain [[Ligures]] known as Epanterii.
[[File:View of Ceva 1835.png|thumb|upright=0.8|left|Ceva in 1835]]
The upper Val Tanaro was [[Ancient Rome|Romanized]] in the second century BC and it is known that the area was organized around a ''[[municipium]]''. However, it is not certain that this was Ceba: [[Mombasiglio]] is also regarded as a candidate. In the first century AD [[Lucius Columella|Columella]] referred to a particular breed of cattle raised here, and [[Pliny the Elder]] praised its sheep's milk cheese in his ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Natural History]]''. The town is on the site of the old Roman road from [[Augusta Taurinorum]] via [[Pollentia]] to the coast{{sfn|Chisholm|1911}} and it is probable that there was a market here from which the cheese produced in the region was exported to Rome via the Ligurian ports of [[Vada Sabatia]] (the modern [[Vado Ligure]]) and/or [[Albingaunum]] (Albenga).

In the [[Middle Ages]] it was the seat of [[Marquisate of Ceva|a small marquisate]], which lasted until the late 15th century when it was acquired by [[duchy of Savoy|Savoy]]. Ceva was home to a fortress defending the confines of Piedmont towards [[Liguria]], but the fortifications on the rock above the town were demolished in 1800 by the [[France|French]], to whom it had been ceded in 1796.<ref>{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Ceva|volume=5|page=777}}</ref>

Ceva was heavily damaged by a flood of the [[Tanaro]], Cevetta and Bovina rivers.

==Napoleonic Era==
During the beginning of [[Napoleon Bonaparte's]] military career in the Italian Campaign, he captured and used Ceva as a point to outflank the [[Piedmontese]] garrison at Cuni in April of 1796. Napoleon's presence in Ceva also threatened [[Turin]] greatly, allowing Napoleon to use Ceva as another launch point for an invasion of [[Turin]]. <ref>Griess, Thomas E., Ed. ''West Point Atlas for The Wars of Napoleon''. Wayne, NJ: Square One Publishers, 2003. </ref>

==Main sights==
The 16th-century castle of the [[Pallavicini family|Pallavicino]] stands in an area of green parkland between the Tanaro and the Cevetta and comprises two small palaces: the original, red ''palazzina rossa'' and the later, white ''palazzina bianca''. Remains of the 16th-century fort are also present.

The [[Duomo of Ceva]], also known as the Collegiata dell'Assunzione della Beata Vergine Maria, was completed in 1605.
